variants.question: digit d in a positive integer is dominant if at least half of the digits in the integer are the digit d. How many positive integers less than or equal to 2026 have at least one dominant digit?
variants.solution: Answer: 867integers. Consider four categories of integers in the span 1 .. 2026: 1. 1 .. 99: Any one digit in any of these values corresponds to at least half of the digits in the value, so is dominant. All 99 such values qualify as having a dominant digit. 2. 100 .. 999: If any two of the three digits in a value match, the value qualifies, but counting these involves multiple subcategories. The non-qualifying values are equivalent to those values that have all digits being different—no matches —which are very easy to count: There are 9 option s (1 .. 9, as 0 does not work for a 3-digit number) for the 100s digit, 9 options left (bringing in 0 but dropping the 100s digit) for the 10s digit, and 8 options left for the 1s digit. Thus, 9 × 9 × 8 = 648 of the 999 − 99 = 900 candidates fail to qualify, so 900 − 648 = 252 qualify. 3. 1000 .. 1999: Like category 2, having any two digits match makes that digit value dominant, so we will again count all of the values in the span that that have all digits being different. The 1000s digit has only the 1 option (1), so there are 9 options left (all other than 1) for the 100s digit, 8 options left for the 10s digit, and 7 options left for the 1s digit. Thus, 1 × 9 × 8 × 7 = 504 of the 1999 − 999 = 1000 possibilities fail to qualify, leaving 1000 − 504 = 496 to qualify. 4. 2000 .. 2026: At least half of the digits in each of 2000 .. 2010 are 0, making 0 the dominant digit and qualifying these 11 values. Then 2011 and 2012 have half 1s and half 2s, respectively, for 2 more qualifying values. At least half of the digits in each of 2020 .. 2026 are 2, making 2 the dominant digit and qualifying these 7 values, so 11 + 2 + 7 = 20 values in this category qualify. In total, there are 99 + 252 + 496 + 20 =𝟏𝟏𝟔𝟔𝟕𝟕 qualifying values. 2026 CHAPTER COMPETITION Solutions

Therefore, let’s use the complement approach and subtract the configuration counts in the two unachievable categories [1 and 2] from the total count of 81. For category 1, all walls are of any 1 of the 3 colors for 3 configurations. For category 2, any 1 of the 4 walls may be painted any 1 of the 3 colors, and all 3 remaining walls are painted a second color, of which 2 choices remain, yielding 4 × 3 × 2 = 24 configurations. variants.question: How many ordered pairs of two-digit positive integers (a, b) are there such that pairs gcd(30, a, b) × lcm(30, a, b) = 30ab?
variants.solution: Answer: 388 (integers) 30.. For all positive integers 𝑚𝑚 and 𝑛𝑛, gcd(𝑚𝑚, 𝑛𝑛) ⋅ lcm(𝑚𝑚, 𝑛𝑛) = 𝑚𝑚𝑛𝑛 , so it i s reasonable to ask if the same concept works upon bring ing in a third positive integer 𝑙𝑙 : gcd(𝑙𝑙, 𝑚𝑚, 𝑛𝑛) ⋅ lcm(𝑙𝑙, 𝑚𝑚, 𝑛𝑛) = 𝑙𝑙𝑚𝑚𝑛𝑛 ? No, that typically does not work—let’s see why not, and what is the most general case that will work for three input values. Let’s focus on a n arbitrary prime factor 𝑝𝑝 , and say that 𝑙𝑙 has 𝑥𝑥 factors of 𝑝𝑝 (that is, 𝑝𝑝 𝑥𝑥 divides 𝑙𝑙 but 𝑝𝑝 𝑥𝑥+1 does not), 𝑚𝑚 has 𝑦𝑦 factors of 𝑝𝑝 , and 𝑛𝑛 has 𝑧𝑧 factors of 𝑝𝑝, with 𝑥𝑥 , 𝑦𝑦, and 𝑧𝑧 being nonnegative integers. Then gcd(𝑚𝑚, 𝑛𝑛) has a factor 𝑝𝑝 min( 𝑦𝑦, 𝑧𝑧) and lcm(𝑚𝑚, 𝑛𝑛) has a factor 𝑝𝑝max(𝑦𝑦, 𝑧𝑧) , so the product of the gcd and lcm has min(𝑦𝑦, 𝑧𝑧) + max(𝑦𝑦, 𝑧𝑧) = 𝑦𝑦 + 𝑧𝑧 factors of 𝑝𝑝, which is the number of factors of 𝑝𝑝 in 𝑚𝑚𝑛𝑛—this always works when two values are being processed. Going to three values, gcd(𝑙𝑙, 𝑚𝑚, 𝑛𝑛) has a factor 𝑝𝑝 min( 𝑥𝑥, 𝑦𝑦, 𝑧𝑧) and lcm(𝑙𝑙, 𝑚𝑚, 𝑛𝑛) has a factor 𝑝𝑝 max(𝑥𝑥, 𝑦𝑦, 𝑧𝑧) , so the product of the gcd and lcm has min(𝑥𝑥, 𝑦𝑦, 𝑧𝑧) + max(𝑥𝑥, 𝑦𝑦, 𝑧𝑧) factors of 𝑝𝑝, while the product 𝑙𝑙 𝑚𝑚𝑛𝑛 has 𝑥𝑥 + 𝑦𝑦 + 𝑧𝑧 factors of 𝑝𝑝—for the two sums to be equal , the middle value 𝑥𝑥 + 𝑦𝑦 + 𝑧𝑧 − (min(𝑥𝑥, 𝑦𝑦, 𝑧𝑧) + max(𝑥𝑥, 𝑦𝑦, 𝑧𝑧)) must be 0, which then requires the minimum value to be 0; in other words, at most one of 𝑥𝑥 , 𝑦𝑦, and 𝑧𝑧 can be nonzero, so 𝑝𝑝 can divide at most one of 𝑙𝑙 , 𝑚𝑚, and 𝑛𝑛—then, and only then, the formula given by the problem can work. Thus, for the given problem with the three values 30 , 𝑎𝑎, and 𝑏𝑏 , no two of those values can have a common divisor greater than 1, thus gcd(30, 𝑎𝑎) = gcd(30, 𝑏𝑏) = gcd(𝑎𝑎, 𝑏𝑏) = 1, which is referred to mathematically as “30, 𝑎𝑎 , and 𝑏𝑏 are mutually relatively prime”. Because 30 = 2 × 3 × 5, 𝑎𝑎 and 𝑏𝑏 must not have any of 2, 3, or 5 as factors. Now, 10 ≤ 𝑎𝑎 ≤ 99 and 10 ≤ 𝑏𝑏 ≤ 99 are given as restrictions. Thus, 𝑎𝑎 and 𝑏𝑏 are required to be [1] distinct 2 -digit primes or [2] the product of primes with the product having two digits. In c ase [1], there are 21 two-digit primes (25 primes under 100 minus 4 primes under 10), so 𝑎𝑎 can be any one of those 21 primes and 𝑏𝑏 can be any of the 20 remaining primes, so 21 × 20 = 420 choices. Case [2] must involve the square of a one- digit prime (other than 2, 3, or 5—meaning 7) or the product of a one-digit prime and a small two - digit prime, leaving only 7² = 49, 7 × 11 = 77, and 7 × 13 = 91 for one of 𝑎𝑎 and 𝑏𝑏, with one of the remaining two-digit primes for the other, thus another 2 × (21 + 20 + 20) = 122 choices. Therefore, the total count of choices is 420 + 122 = 542.
